claim: Δ9-tetrahydrocannabinol disrupts autophagy selectively in the striatum both in vitro and in vivo
source: Here, we found that Δ9-tetrahydrocannabinol, the psychoactive ingredient of cannabis, disrupts autophagy selectively in the striatum, a brain area that controls motor behavior, both in vitro and in vivo.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from Western blot and immunofluorescence analyses showing THC-induced accumulation of LC3-II and p62 in striatum but not other brain regions (Figures 1, 2)

claim: Boosting autophagy pharmacologically with temsirolimus rescues the Δ9-tetrahydrocannabinol-induced impairment of motor coordination in mice
source: Boosting autophagy, either pharmacologically (with temsirolimus) or by dietary intervention (with trehalose), rescued the Δ9-tetrahydrocannabinol-induced impairment of motor coordination in mice.
evidence: Supported by RotaRod test data showing temsirolimus prevented THC-induced motor coordination impairment (Figure 3A)

claim: Boosting autophagy by dietary intervention with trehalose rescues the Δ9-tetrahydrocannabinol-induced impairment of motor coordination in mice
source: Boosting autophagy, either pharmacologically (with temsirolimus) or by dietary intervention (with trehalose), rescued the Δ9-tetrahydrocannabinol-induced impairment of motor coordination in mice.
evidence: Supported by RotaRod test data showing trehalose prevented THC-induced motor coordination impairment (Figure 4A)

claim: Cannabinoid CB1 receptors located on neurons belonging to the direct (striatonigral) pathway are required for the motor-impairing activity of Δ9-tetrahydrocannabinol
source: The combination of conditional knockout mouse models and viral vector-mediated autophagy-modulating strategies in vivo showed that cannabinoid CB1 receptors located on neurons belonging to the direct (striatonigral) pathway are required for the motor-impairing activity of Δ9-tetrahydrocannabinol by inhibiting local autophagy.
evidence: Supported by data from D1R-CB1R KO mice showing absence of THC-induced motor impairment and autophagy disruption (Figure 5A-C)

claim: Cannabinoid CB1 receptors located on neurons belonging to the direct pathway inhibit local autophagy
source: The combination of conditional knockout mouse models and viral vector-mediated autophagy-modulating strategies in vivo showed that cannabinoid CB1 receptors located on neurons belonging to the direct (striatonigral) pathway are required for the motor-impairing activity of Δ9-tetrahydrocannabinol by inhibiting local autophagy.
evidence: Supported by Western blot and immunofluorescence data showing THC-induced autophagy markers in CB1R-floxed but not D1R-CB1R KO mice (Figure 5B-C)

claim: Cannabis is one of the most common drugs of abuse in the world
source: Cannabis is one of the most common drugs of abuse in the world (Alpár et al., 2016; Englund et al., 2017; Volkow et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature

claim: Δ9-tetrahydrocannabinol is the third most popular recreational addictive chemical following ethanol and nicotine
source: Consequently, its major intoxicating constituent, the cannabinoid Δ9-tetrahydrocannabinol (THC), is the third most popular recreational addictive chemical following ethanol and nicotine.
evidence: Based on inference from cannabis being one of the most common drugs of abuse

claim: Several states in the USA and a few countries in the world have legalized the recreational use of cannabis
source: Of note, several states in the USA, as well as a few countries in the world, have legalized the recreational use of cannabis.
evidence: Statement of fact about legal status, based on general knowledge

claim: THC and other cannabinoids are approved by various regulatory agencies as anti-emetic, anti-cachexic, analgesic and anti-spastic compounds
source: In this context, THC and other cannabinoids are already approved by various regulatory agencies, including the Food and Drug Administration (FDA), the European Medicines Agency and Health Canada, as anti-emetic, anti-cachexic, analgesic and anti-spastic compounds (Hill, 2015; Whiting et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature

claim: Medical-grade cannabis dispensation programs have been implemented in about half of the states in the USA and in a growing number of countries globally
source: Moreover, medical-grade cannabis dispensation programs have been implemented in about half of the states in the USA and in a growing number of countries globally.
evidence: Statement of fact about medical cannabis programs, based on general knowledge

claim: Cannabis use is associated to several undesired and possibly dangerous side effects
source: However, cannabis use is associated to several undesired and possibly dangerous side effects, so it is crucial that innovative procedures aimed to understand and potentially reduce cannabis-evoked harms are explored (Alpár et al., 2016; Englund et al., 2017; Volkow et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature

claim: THC exerts its biological effects mainly by activating cannabinoid CB1 receptor
source: THC exerts its biological effects mainly by activating cannabinoid CB1 receptor, one of the most abundant metabotropic receptors in the mammalian central nervous system (Katona and Freund, 2008; Pertwee et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature

claim: CB1 receptor is one of the most abundant metabotropic receptors in the mammalian central nervous system
source: THC exerts its biological effects mainly by activating cannabinoid CB1 receptor, one of the most abundant metabotropic receptors in the mammalian central nervous system (Katona and Freund, 2008; Pertwee et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature

claim: CB1 receptor is particularly expressed in discrete brain areas involved in the control of learning and memory, motor behavior, emotions, and autonomic and endocrine functions
source: This receptor is particularly expressed in discrete brain areas involved in the control of learning and memory (cortex, hippocampus), motor behavior (striatum, cerebellum), emotions (amygdala), and autonomic and endocrine functions (hypothalamus, pons, medulla), therefore participating in the control of a wide plethora of biological processes (Katona and Freund, 2008; Mechoulam and Parker, 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature

claim: Endocannabinoids biologically engage the CB1 receptor, mediating a feedback mechanism aimed to prevent excessive neuronal activity
source: A family of retrograde lipid messengers, the endocannabinoids, biologically engages the CB1 receptor, mediating a feedback mechanism aimed to prevent excessive neuronal activity and, thereby, tuning the functionality and plasticity of many synapses (Castillo et al., 2012; Piomelli, 2003).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature

claim: The CB1 receptor can control autophagy
source: Recent evidence suggests that the CB1 receptor can control autophagy, a highly conserved and pleiotropic process of cellular 'self-digestion' in which cytoplasmic materials are sequestered into double-membrane vesicles called autophagosomes, and subsequently delivered to lysosomes for degradation or recycling (Costa et al., 2016; Hiebel and Behl, 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature

claim: Autophagy is an essential mechanism of cellular quality control
source: Autophagy is an essential mechanism of cellular quality control, and the knowledge on its biological functions in the brain and other organs is rapidly increasing (Menzies et al., 2017; Ohsumi, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature

claim: In some cell-culture settings cannabinoids via the CB1 receptor enhance autophagy
source: Strikingly, in some cell-culture settings cannabinoids via the CB1 receptor enhance autophagy (Koay et al., 2014; Salazar et al., 2009), while in others they inhibit autophagy (Hiebel et al., 2014; Piyanova et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature

claim: In some cell-culture settings cannabinoids via the CB1 receptor inhibit autophagy
source: Strikingly, in some cell-culture settings cannabinoids via the CB1 receptor enhance autophagy (Koay et al., 2014; Salazar et al., 2009), while in others they inhibit autophagy (Hiebel et al., 2014; Piyanova et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature

claim: THC increased LC3-II levels in the striatum but not in the cortex, hippocampus, or cerebellum
source: THC increased LC3-II levels in the striatum, either when referred to LC3-I (THC vs. vehicle, t = 4.680; df = 10; p=0.0009) or to β-actin (THC vs. vehicle, t = 4.331; df = 10; p=0.0015) as control, but not in other representative brain regions as the cortex, the hippocampus and the cerebellum (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by Western blot data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 1A

claim: THC induced an accumulation of p62 in the striatum but not in other brain regions tested
source: THC induced an accumulation of p62 in the striatum (THC vs. vehicle, t = 5.303; df = 10; p=0.0003), but not in the other brain regions tested (Figure 1A), thus indicating that THC impairs the execution of autophagy and that this process occurs selectively in the striatum.
evidence: Supported by Western blot data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 1A

claim: The levels of LC3-I and p62 were not significantly different in the striatum than in the cortex, hippocampus or cerebellum from vehicle-treated mice
source: Of note, the levels of LC3-I and p62 were not significantly different in the striatum than in the cortex, hippocampus or cerebellum from vehicle-treated mice (Figure 1B), suggesting that the selective impact of THC on striatal autophagy does not rely on the basal expression of those two key autophagy proteins but on additional, hitherto unknown molecular factors.
evidence: Supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 1B

claim: THC and HU-210 increased LC3-II levels in primary striatal neurons
source: The two cannabinoid drugs increased LC3-II levels, as determined by immunofluorescence (aggregated-LC3 puncta), in both the total intracellular compartment (F(2,28) = 39.48; THC vs. vehicle, p=0.0004; HU-210 vs. vehicle, p<0.0001) and the lysosomal compartment, as identified by the lysosomal marker LAMP1 (F(2,28) = 22.43; THC vs. vehicle, p<0.0001, HU-210 vs. vehicle: p<0.0001) (Figure 2A).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 2A

claim: THC and HU-210 enhanced p62 levels in primary striatal neurons
source: Concertedly, they also enhanced p62 levels (F(2,30) = 38.81; THC vs. vehicle, p=0.0130; HU-210 vs. vehicle, p=0.0335) (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 2B

claim: Cannabinoids did not significantly heighten LC3-II and p62 levels pre-augmented by lysosomal inhibitors in striatal neurons
source: Of note, cannabinoids did not significantly heighten those pre-augmented levels of LC3-II (Figure 2A) and p62 (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2A and 2B

claim: THC impaired motor coordination as determined by the RotaRod test
source: Four hours after injection, THC impaired motor coordination, as determined by the RotaRod test, and temsirolimus, under conditions that did not influence behavior by itself, rescued the effect of THC (F(3,30) = 6.635; THC vs. vehicle, p=0.0016; temsirolimus + THC vs. THC, p=0.0096) (Figure 3A).
evidence: Supported by RotaRod test data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 3A

claim: Temsirolimus rescued the THC-induced impairment of motor coordination
source: Four hours after injection, THC impaired motor coordination, as determined by the RotaRod test, and temsirolimus, under conditions that did not influence behavior by itself, rescued the effect of THC (F(3,30) = 6.635; THC vs. vehicle, p=0.0016; temsirolimus + THC vs. THC, p=0.0096) (Figure 3A).
evidence: Supported by RotaRod test data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 3A

claim: The inhibitory action of THC on general locomotor activity was not significantly affected by temsirolimus
source: In contrast, the inhibitory action of THC on general locomotor activity, as determined by various parameters in the open field test (THC vs. vehicle, ambulation: F(3,24) = 24.14; p=0.0002; activity: F(3,24) = 10.67; p=0.0241; resting time: F(3,24) = 13.89; p=0.0067; fast movements: F(3,24) = 14.15; p=0.0002; stereotypic movements: F(3,24) = 8.240; p=0.0137), was not significantly affected by temsirolimus (Figure 3—figure supplement 1; Puighermanal et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by open field test data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1

claim: THC concomitantly inhibited autophagy and activated the mTORC1 pathway in mouse striata
source: Under these experimental conditions, western blot analysis of mouse striata supported that THC concomitantly inhibited autophagy, as determined by the simultaneous accumulation of LC3-II (THC vs. vehicle, F(3,12) = 10.77; p=0.0119) and p62 (THC vs. vehicle, F(3,12) = 12.29; p=0.0017) (Figure 3B), and activated the mTORC1 pathway, as determined by an enhanced phosphorylation of the mTORC1-dependent sites in two of its main substrates, namely T389 in 70 kDa ribosomal protein S6 kinase (S6K) (THC vs. vehicle, F(3,12) = 28.70; p=0.0009), and S757 in ULK1 (THC vs. vehicle, F(3,12) = 8.506; p=0.0214) (Figure 3C).
evidence: Supported by Western blot data and statistical analysis shown in Figures 3B and 3C

claim: Temsirolimus rescued the THC-evoked effects on p62 and mTORC1 pathway markers
source: Of note, temsirolimus rescued these cannabinoid-evoked effects on p62 (temsirolimus + THC vs. THC, F(3,12) = 12.29; p=0.0008) (Figure 3B) and the mTORC1 pathway markers (pS6K-T389: temsirolimus + THC vs. THC, F(3,12) = 28.70; p<0.0001. pULK1-S757: temsirolimus + THC vs. THC, F(3,12) = 8.506; p=0.0470) (Figure 3C).
evidence: Supported by Western blot data and statistical analysis shown in Figures 3B and 3C

claim: The phosphorylation state of the main AMPK-dependent site in ULK1 (S555) was not significantly affected by THC and/or temsirolimus
source: As a control, we found that the phosphorylation state of the main AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK)-dependent site in ULK1, namely S555, was not significantly affected by THC and/or temsirolimus (Figure 3C).
evidence: Supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 3C

claim: Trehalose rescued the THC-evoked impairment of motor coordination
source: Trehalose, under conditions that did not affect behavior by itself, rescued the THC-evoked impairment of motor coordination (F(3,45) = 3.858; THC vs. vehicle, p=0.0321; trehalose + THC vs. THC, p=0.0358) (Figure 4A).
evidence: Supported by RotaRod test data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 4A

claim: The inhibitory action of THC on general locomotor activity was not significantly affected by trehalose
source: As shown above for temsirolimus, the inhibitory action of THC on general locomotor activity, as determined by various parameters in the open field test (THC vs. vehicle, ambulation: F(3,27) = 7.548; p=0.0402; activity: F(3,27) = 8.536; p=0.0134; resting time: F(3,27) = 7.420; p=0.0154; fast movements: F(3,27) = 8.496; p=0.0356; stereotypic movements: F(3,27) = 9.173; p=0.0032), was not significantly affected by trehalose (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by open field test data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1

claim: Trehalose reduced the THC-induced accumulation of striatal p62
source: Western blot analysis of mouse striata indicated that trehalose reduced the THC-induced accumulation of striatal p62 (F(3,12) = 23.66; THC vs. vehicle, p=0.0017; trehalose + THC vs. THC, p<0.0001) (Figure 4B).
evidence: Supported by Western blot data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 4B

claim: Trehalose mitigated the THC-evoked stimulation of the mTORC1 pathway
source: Trehalose per se did not significantly affect mTORC1 activity markers, but mitigated the THC-evoked stimulation of the pathway (pS6K-T389: F(3,12) = 5.410; THC vs. vehicle, p=0.0388; trehalose + THC vs. THC, p=0.1944. pULK1-S757: F(3,12) = 12.03; THC vs. vehicle, p=0.0032; trehalose + THC vs. THC, p=0.0074) (Figure 4C).
evidence: Supported by Western blot data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 4C

claim: ULK1-S555 phosphorylation was not significantly affected by THC and/or trehalose
source: ULK1-S555 phosphorylation was not significantly affected by THC and/or trehalose (Figure 4C).
evidence: Supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 4C

claim: Rimonabant abrogated the THC-evoked impairment of motor coordination
source: Four hours after injection, THC impaired RotaRod performance, and rimonabant, under conditions that did not influence behavior by itself, abrogated the effect of THC (F(3,16) = 12.86; THC vs. vehicle, p=0.0020; rimonabant + THC vs. THC, p=0.0002) (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by RotaRod test data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1

claim: The motor-dyscoordinating action of THC found in CB1R-floxed mice was not evident in D1R-CB1R KO animals
source: Remarkably, the motor-dyscoordinating action of THC (10 mg/kg, i.p.) found in CB1R-floxed mice was not evident in D1R-CB1R KO animals (F(3,18) = 6.571; CB1R-floxed-THC vs. CB1R-floxed-vehicle, p=0.0067; D1R-CB1R KO-THC vs. CB1R-floxed-THC, p=0.0068) (Figure 5A).
evidence: Supported by RotaRod test data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 5A

claim: The simultaneous accumulation of LC3-II and p62 evoked by THC in control mice was not observed in D1R-CB1R KO mice
source: In concert, the simultaneous accumulation of LC3-II and p62 evoked by THC in control mice, as assessed by western blot, was not observed in D1R-CB1R KO mice (LC3-II: F(3,12) = 6.981; CB1R-floxed-THC vs. CB1R-floxed-vehicle, p=0.0066; D1R-CB1R KO-THC vs. CB1R-floxed-THC, p=0.0122. p62: F(3,12) = 13.36; CB1R-floxed-THC vs. CB1R-floxed-vehicle, p=0.0014; D1R-CB1R KO-THC vs. CB1R-floxed-THC, p=0.0005) (Figure 5B).
evidence: Supported by Western blot data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 5B

claim: Administration of THC decreased RotaRod performance comparably in Glu-CB1R KO mice and their control CB1R-floxed littermates
source: Administration of THC (10 mg/kg, i.p.) decreased RotaRod performance comparably in Glu-CB1R KO mice and their control CB1R-floxed littermates (F(3,12) = 65.18; CB1R-floxed-THC vs. CB1R-floxed-vehicle, p<0.0001; Glu-CB1R KO-THC vs. Glu-CB1R KO-vehicle, p<0.0001) (Figure 5D).
evidence: Supported by RotaRod test data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 5D

claim: THC enhanced LC3-II and p62 levels similarly in Glu-CB1R KO and CB1R-floxed mice
source: Likewise, as assessed by western blot, THC enhanced LC3-II and p62 levels similarly in Glu-CB1R KO and CB1R-floxed mice (LC3-II: F(3,12) = 9.471; CB1R-floxed-THC vs. CB1R-floxed-vehicle, p=0.0182; Glu-CB1R KO-THC vs. Glu-CB1R KO-vehicle, p=0.0107. p62: F(3,12) = 9.462; CB1R-floxed-THC vs. CB1R-floxed-vehicle, p=0.0093; Glu-CB1R KO-THC vs. Glu-CB1R KO-vehicle, p=0.0168) (Figure 5E).
evidence: Supported by Western blot data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 5E

claim: The THC-induced activation of the mTORC1 pathway occurred selectively in D1R-MSNs
source: Four hours later, immunofluorescence analysis revealed that the THC-induced activation of the mTORC1 pathway (as determined by protein S6 phosphorylation) occurred selectively in D1R-MSNs (F(3,15) = 7.387; D1R-MSN-THC vs. D1R-MSN-vehicle, p=0.0058; D2R-MSN-THC vs. D1R-MSN-THC, p=0.0146) (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1

claim: Dominant-negative Raptor prevented the THC-induced impairment of motor coordination
source: Dominant-negative Raptor did not affect RotaRod performance in vehicle-treated animals, but prevented the THC-induced impairment of motor coordination (F(7,28) = 5.309; THC-WT/post-treatment vs. vehicle-WT/post-treatment, p=0.0010; THC-D1R-Cre/post-treatment vs. THC-WT/post-treatment, p=0.0034) (Figure 6A).
evidence: Supported by RotaRod test data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 6A

claim: p62 overexpression per se decreased RotaRod performance in vehicle-treated animals
source: Of note, p62 overexpression per se decreased RotaRod performance in vehicle-treated animals, and this decrease was not additive to that induced by THC administration (10 mg/kg, i.p.) (F(7,28) = 5.641; THC-WT/post-treatment vs. vehicle-WT/post-treatment, p=0.0152; vehicle-D1R-Cre/pre-treatment vs. vehicle-WT/pre-treatment, p=0.0477; THC-D1R-Cre/pre-treatment vs. THC-WT/pre-treatment, p=0.0450) (Figure 6B).
evidence: Supported by RotaRod test data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 6B

claim: The decrease in RotaRod performance from p62 overexpression was not additive to that induced by THC administration
source: Of note, p62 overexpression per se decreased RotaRod performance in vehicle-treated animals, and this decrease was not additive to that induced by THC administration (10 mg/kg, i.p.) (F(7,28) = 5.641; THC-WT/post-treatment vs. vehicle-WT/post-treatment, p=0.0152; vehicle-D1R-Cre/pre-treatment vs. vehicle-WT/pre-treatment, p=0.0477; THC-D1R-Cre/pre-treatment vs. THC-WT/pre-treatment, p=0.0450) (Figure 6B).
evidence: Supported by RotaRod test data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 6B

claim: Inhibition of autophagy is an unprecedented mechanistic link between cannabinoids and motor performance
source: Taken together, these findings identify inhibition of autophagy as an unprecedented mechanistic link between cannabinoids and motor performance, and suggest that activators of autophagy might be considered as potential therapeutic tools to treat specific cannabinoid-evoked behavioral alterations.
evidence: Based on inference from the experimental data showing THC inhibits autophagy and impairs motor coordination, and that autophagy activators rescue this effect

claim: Activators of autophagy might be considered as potential therapeutic tools to treat specific cannabinoid-evoked behavioral alterations
source: Taken together, these findings identify inhibition of autophagy as an unprecedented mechanistic link between cannabinoids and motor performance, and suggest that activators of autophagy might be considered as potential therapeutic tools to treat specific cannabinoid-evoked behavioral alterations.
evidence: Speculative statement based on the experimental findings with temsirolimus and trehalose

claim: CB1 receptor activation by coupling to the phosphatidylinositol-3-kinase/Akt/mTORC1 pathway would lead to ULK1 phosphorylation, which would inhibit autophagosome formation
source: First, CB1 receptor activation, by coupling to the phosphatidylinositol-3-kinase/Akt/mTORC1 pathway, would lead to ULK1 phosphorylation, which, subsequently, would inhibit autophagosome formation/autophagy initiation.
evidence: Based on inference from the experimental data showing THC activates mTORC1 and phosphorylates ULK1

claim: CB1 receptor activation by a hitherto undefined mechanism would inhibit autophagosome clearance
source: Second, CB1 receptor activation, by a hitherto undefined mechanism that may conceivably involve an impact on lysosomal function (Hiebel and Behl, 2015), would inhibit autophagosome clearance/autophagy completion.
evidence: Speculative statement based on the accumulation of LC3-II and p62, with citation to support potential lysosomal involvement

claim: Temsirolimus prevents other unwanted effects of THC, such as short-term memory loss and anxiety
source: Temsirolimus prevents other unwanted effects of THC, such as short-term memory loss and anxiety, leaving potential therapeutically sought cannabinoid actions as analgesia and anxiolysis unaffected (Puighermanal et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature

claim: Temsirolimus has similar potency and specificity for mTOR than rapamycin, but longer stability and increased solubility
source: Temsirolimus has similar potency and specificity for mTOR than rapamycin, but longer stability and increased solubility, and is already approved by the FDA as first-line treatment for metastatic renal cancer patients classified as poor risk (Hudes et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature

claim: Temsirolimus is approved by the FDA as first-line treatment for metastatic renal cancer patients classified as poor risk
source: Temsirolimus has similar potency and specificity for mTOR than rapamycin, but longer stability and increased solubility, and is already approved by the FDA as first-line treatment for metastatic renal cancer patients classified as poor risk (Hudes et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature

claim: In metastatic renal cancer patients, temsirolimus is well-tolerated, increases overall survival, and improves quality of life
source: In these patients, temsirolimus is well-tolerated, increases overall survival, and improves quality of life (Zanardi et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature

claim: Administration of temsirolimus or other FDA-approved rapalogs like everolimus might help to counteract some particular unwanted effects of cannabis
source: Taken together, these pieces of evidence suggest that administration of temsirolimus, or other FDA-approved rapalogs like everolimus (Janku et al., 2018; Lebwohl et al., 2013), might help to counteract some particular unwanted effects of cannabis.
evidence: Speculative statement based on the experimental findings and cited literature

claim: Trehalose is a nontoxic disaccharide found in numerous plants, microorganisms and invertebrates
source: Trehalose, a nontoxic disaccharide found in numerous plants, microorganisms and invertebrates, contains an α,α−1,1-glucoside bond between two α-glucose units, thus being an extremely stable sugar.
evidence: Statement based on established scientific knowledge

claim: In many countries, including USA, trehalose is added to various food products as nutritional supplement and 'natural flavor'
source: In many countries, including USA, trehalose is added to various food products as nutritional supplement and 'natural flavor' (Richards et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature

claim: Trehalose is believed to stabilize proteins and to protect them from stress-induced unfolding, aggregation and degradation
source: On physiological grounds, trehalose is believed to stabilize proteins and to protect them from stress-induced unfolding, aggregation and degradation (Emanuele, 2014; Hosseinpour-Moghaddam et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature

claim: Vertebrates cannot synthesize trehalose
source: Vertebrates cannot synthesize trehalose, but exogenous trehalose administration induces the clearance of toxic protein aggregates in cultured mammalian cells, and exerts therapeutic effects in a plethora of mouse models of protein-misfolding disorders (including Huntington's disease, Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease and amyotrophic lateral sclerosis) concomitantly to autophagy induction (Hosseinpour-Moghaddam et al., 2018; Menzies et al., 2017).
evidence: Statement based on established scientific knowledge

claim: Exogenous trehalose administration induces the clearance of toxic protein aggregates in cultured mammalian cells
source: Vertebrates cannot synthesize trehalose, but exogenous trehalose administration induces the clearance of toxic protein aggregates in cultured mammalian cells, and exerts therapeutic effects in a plethora of mouse models of protein-misfolding disorders (including Huntington's disease, Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease and amyotrophic lateral sclerosis) concomitantly to autophagy induction (Hosseinpour-Moghaddam et al., 2018; Menzies et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature

claim: Trehalose exerts therapeutic effects in mouse models of protein-misfolding disorders concomitantly to autophagy induction
source: Vertebrates cannot synthesize trehalose, but exogenous trehalose administration induces the clearance of toxic protein aggregates in cultured mammalian cells, and exerts therapeutic effects in a plethora of mouse models of protein-misfolding disorders (including Huntington's disease, Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease and amyotrophic lateral sclerosis) concomitantly to autophagy induction (Hosseinpour-Moghaddam et al., 2018; Menzies et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature

claim: Trehalose has been proposed to activate autophagy via competitive inhibition of GLUT glucose transporters, thus impairing cellular energy supply and stimulating AMPK
source: Although its mechanism of action is not completely understood (Lee et al., 2018), trehalose has been proposed to activate autophagy via competitive inhibition of GLUT glucose transporters, thus impairing cellular energy supply and stimulating AMPK (DeBosch et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature

claim: The CB1 receptor is one of the most abundant metabotropic receptors in the striatum
source: The CB1 receptor is one of the most abundant metabotropic receptors in the striatum, where it is mainly expressed in D1R-MSNs, D2R-MSNs, GABAergic interneurons, and astrocytes, as well as in glutamatergic terminals projecting from the cortex (Castillo et al., 2012; Davis et al., 2018; Uchigashima et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature

claim: CB1 receptor is mainly expressed in D1R-MSNs, D2R-MSNs, GABAergic interneurons, and astrocytes, as well as in glutamatergic terminals projecting from the cortex in the striatum
source: The CB1 receptor is one of the most abundant metabotropic receptors in the striatum, where it is mainly expressed in D1R-MSNs, D2R-MSNs, GABAergic interneurons, and astrocytes, as well as in glutamatergic terminals projecting from the cortex (Castillo et al., 2012; Davis et al., 2018; Uchigashima et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature

claim: The pool of CB1 receptors located on D1R-MSNs is necessary for cannabinoid-induced catalepsy
source: Of note, it has been shown that this precise CB1 receptor subpopulation is also necessary for cannabinoid-induced catalepsy, although not for overall cannabinoid-induced hypomotility (Monory et al., 2007), thus supporting that, in agreement with our data, it controls selected aspects of motor behavior.
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature

claim: The pool of CB1 receptors located on D1R-MSNs is not necessary for overall cannabinoid-induced hypomotility
source: Of note, it has been shown that this precise CB1 receptor subpopulation is also necessary for cannabinoid-induced catalepsy, although not for overall cannabinoid-induced hypomotility (Monory et al., 2007), thus supporting that, in agreement with our data, it controls selected aspects of motor behavior.
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature

claim: CB1 receptors located on corticostriatal terminals contribute to THC-induced hypolocomotion

claim: An increase of LC3-II together with a decrease of p62 usually denotes an increased autophagic flux
